This week-long 2010 search across Tyne and Wear and Northumberland for the fugitive Raoul Moat ended in his suicide near Rothbury after a six-hour standoff with armed officers — what is this event called?
2010 Northumbria Police manhunt was conducted across Tyne and Wear and Northumberland from 3 to 10 July 2010 with the objective of apprehending fugitive Raoul Moat.
This ancient Iranic nomadic people migrated to the North Caucasus, with some continuing into Europe and North Africa, and are regarded as part of the Sarmatians — name the people?
Alans were an ancient and medieval Iranic nomadic pastoral people who migrated to what is today the North Caucasus; some continued on to Europe and later North Africa.
Ruled from Aigai and later Pella by the Argead dynasty, this Greek-speaking tribe expanded along the Haliacmon valley, absorbing neighboring Thracian and Illyrian peoples — who were they?
Ancient Macedonians (Ancient) were an ancient tribe that lived on the alluvial plain around the rivers Haliacmon and lower Axios in the northeastern part of mainland Greece.
Worshipped across ancient Semitic cultures as a goddess of fertility, motherhood, and sacred trees, this deity was said to be the sea goddess consort of the sky god El — who is she?
Asherah was a goddess in ancient Semitic religions. Asherah was a major goddess in ancient Northwest Semitic cultures, often associated with fertility, motherhood, and sacred trees.
A federal prosecutor turned Delaware attorney general, this Democrat born in 1969 was the firstborn child of a man who'd become the 46th U.S. president — who was he?
Beau Biden (February 3, 1969 - May 30, 2015) was an American politician, lawyer, and Army National Guard officer who served as the 44th attorney general of Delaware from 2007 to 2015.
Known as Perarignar Anna, this Dravidian-party leader and acclaimed Tamil writer led Madras State before dying just 20 days into leading its successor state — who is he?
C. N. Annadurai (15 September 1909 - 3 February 1969), also known as Perarignar Anna, was an Indian politician who was the founder and first general-secretary of the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK).
The longest-serving leader of Germany's Free Democratic Party, he served as federal finance minister from 2021 until his dismissal in 2024 sparked a government crisis — who is he?

Christian Lindner (born 7 January 1979) is a German retired politician of the Free Democratic Party (FDP) who was the Federal Minister of Finance from 2021 until his dismissal in 2024 during a government crisis.

This 19th-century Scottish missionary-doctor explored Africa for the London Missionary Society and became a mythic figure as both an anti-slavery crusader and advocate of British commercial expansion. Who was he?
David Livingstone (19 March 1813 - 1 May 1873) was a Scottish doctor, Congregationalist, pioneer Christian missionary with the London Missionary Society, and an explorer in Africa.
Replacing Władysław Gomułka as First Secretary of the ruling party, which Polish leader had spent his youth in France before returning home in 1948?
Edward Gierek (Polish; 6 January 1913 - 29 July 2001) was a Polish communist politician who served as the de facto leader of the Polish People's Republic between 1970 and 1980.
This Spanish fascist movement, founded in October 1933, merged months later with the JONS group co-founded by Onésimo Redondo — which organization?
Falange Española (FE) was a Spanish fascist and national syndicalist political organization active from 1933 to 1934.

This Indonesian politician governed Central Java for a decade before finishing third in the 2024 presidential race, having earlier spent two terms as a national legislator representing the same province — who is he?
Ganjar Pranowo (born 28 October 1968) is an Indonesian politician who served as the governor of Central Java between 2013 and 2023.
Catherine the Great's lover, favorite, and possibly her consort, this Russian statesman died during the negotiations that ended his war with the Ottomans — who was he?
Grigory Potemkin was Russian military leader and statesman (1739–1791).

Taught to fly by the Wright brothers themselves, this aviation pioneer became the only American to hold five-star rank in two different branches of the military and founded what became the RAND Corporation — who was he?
Henry H. Arnold (25 June 1886 - 15 January 1950) was an American general officer holding the ranks of General of the Army and later, General of the Air Force.
Cambodia's longest-serving head of government, this politician led the country as prime minister across three separate terms totaling nearly four decades before becoming Senate president — who is he?
Hun Sen (born 5 August 1952) is a Cambodian politician and former military officer who currently serves as the president of the Senate.
Which Guatemalan president — son of a Swiss German father — championed a landmark land-reform program that rippled across Latin America before he was toppled in 1954?
Jacobo Árbenz (14 September 1913 - 27 January 1971) was a Guatemalan military officer and politician who served as the 25th president of Guatemala.

A devoted diarist who corresponded for years with both his wife Abigail and his friend-turned-rival Thomas Jefferson, this Founding Father served as the very first U.S. vice president before moving up one chair — who was he?
John Adams (October 30, 1735 - July 4, 1826) was a Founding Father and the second president of the United States from 1797 to 1801.
The only one of Napoleon's siblings allowed back into France after 1815, who later served as President of the Senate in 1852?

Jérôme Bonaparte (born Girolamo Buonaparte; 15 November 1784 - 24 June 1860) was the youngest brother of Napoleon I who reigned as Jrme Napoleon I (formally Hieronymus Napoleon in German), King of Westphalia, between 1807 and 1813.
This German statesman, a devout Catholic who had served as Mayor of Cologne, became the first chancellor of West Germany in 1949 and is remembered as a founding father of the EU — who was he?
Konrad Adenauer (5 January 1876 - 19 April 1967) was a German statesman and politician who served as the first chancellor of West Germany from 1949 to 1963.
This Roman empress divorced her first husband to marry Octavian in 38 BC, and remained his wife when the Senate proclaimed him Augustus nine years later — who was she?
Livia (30 January 59 BC - AD 29) was Roman empress from 27 BC to AD 14 as the wife of Augustus, the first Roman emperor.

Often called 'the richest man in Rome,' this Roman general and statesman began his career as a military commander under Sulla, later amassing an enormous fortune through property speculation — who is he?
Marcus Licinius Crassus (115-53 BC) was a Roman general and statesman who played a key role in the transformation of the Roman Republic into the Roman Empire.

The youngest prime minister in Danish history, this politician became just the second woman to hold the office when she took power in 2019, after earlier serving as both employment and justice minister. Who is she?
Mette Frederiksen (born 19 November 1977) is a Danish politician who has served as the prime minister of Denmark since 2019 and the Leader of the Social Democrats since 2015.
Described by Ovid as the son of Sleep who appears to people in dreams in human form, this figure lent his name to the general concept of the god of dreams — who is he?
Morpheus (Ancient) is a god associated with sleep and dreams.
This British stockbroker quietly arranged the rescue of 669 mostly Jewish children from Czechoslovakia on the eve of World War II, an effort later known as the Czech Kindertransport — who was he?

Nicholas Winton (n Wertheim; 19 May 1909 - 1 July 2015) was a British stockbroker and humanitarian who helped to rescue refugee children, mostly Jewish, whose families had fled persecution by Nazi Germany.
Which brief Roman emperor of 69 AD allied with Galba during the revolts of 68, only to murder him and later face defeat by Vitellius's forces at the Battle of Bedriacum?
Otho (28 April 32 - 16 April 69) was Roman emperor, ruling for three months from 15 January to 16 April 69.
Ruling from the Nubian city of Napata in modern Sudan, this Kushite king founded Egypt's Twenty-fifth Dynasty in the 8th century BC. Who was he?
Piye (also interpreted as Pnkhi, Piankhy, Painkhi, Pinkhi, or Pankhi) was an ancient Kushite king and founder of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty of Egypt, who ruled Egypt during 744-714 BC.
After eight years in the British Army, including counter-insurgency work in Oman, this adventurer became the first person to cross Antarctica entirely on foot — who is he?
Ranulph Fiennes (born 7 March 1944) is an English explorer and writer, who holds several endurance records.
He lost his first run for New York City mayor in 1989, won in 1993, and was reelected in 1997 — which politician was the city's 108th mayor?
Rudy Giuliani (born May 28, 1944) is an American politician and disbarred lawyer who served as the 108th mayor of New York City from 1994 to 2001.
Serving as First Deputy Chief of Staff of the Presidential Administration since 2016, which former Russian prime minister has played a leading role governing Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory?
Sergey Kiriyenko (né Izraitel; born 26 July 1962) is a Russian politician who has served as First Deputy Chief of Staff of the Presidential Administration of Russia since 5 October 2016.
This Italian businessman-turned-politician has run a football club since 2017 and took office as mayor of an Umbrian city in 2023 — who is he?
Stefano Bandecchi (born 4 April 1961) is an Italian politician and entrepreneur.
Born in 42 BC, this second Roman emperor ruled from AD 14 until his death, succeeding his stepfather Augustus — who is he?
Tiberius (ty-; 16 November 42 BC - 16 March AD 37) was Roman emperor from AD 14 until his death, reigning as the second ruler of the Julio-Claudian dynasty.
These Scandinavian seafarers raided, traded, and settled across Europe from the late 8th to 11th centuries, voyaging as far as Greenland and even present-day Newfoundland — who were they?

Vikings were a seafaring people originally from Scandinavia (present-day Denmark, Norway, and Sweden), who from the late 8th to the late 11th centuries raided, pirated, traded, and settled throughout parts of Europe.
Canada's longest-serving prime minister, with three non-consecutive terms totaling over 21 years, he was also the first to hold a PhD. Who was he?
William Lyon Mackenzie King (December 17, 1874 - July 22, 1950) was the tenth prime minister of Canada for three non-consecutive terms from 1921 to 1926, 1926 to 1930, and 1935 to 1948.

First known for a decade-long fight against a toxic landfill in her hometown of Pezinok, which won her the 2016 Goldman Environmental Prize, this activist became Slovakia's first female president in 2019 — who is she?
Zuzana Čaputová (ne Strapkov; born 21 June 1973) is a Slovak politician, lawyer, and environmental activist who served as the fifth president of Slovakia from 2019 to 2024.
Prime Minister during the years Turkey joined NATO and fought in Korea, he became the last Turkish leader executed after a military coup, hanged in 1961 — who was he?
Adnan Menderes: 9th Prime Minister of the Republic of Turkey from 1950 to 1960.

Amal Movement: Lebanese political party. It was founded by Musa al-Sadr and Hussein el-Husseini in 1974 as the "Movement of the Deprived".
Henry VIII's marriage to his fourth wife lasted barely six months in 1540, doomed partly because a portrait by Hans Holbein flattered her more than reality did — who was she?

Assimi Goïta: Leader of Mali (2020; since 2021)

This Hebrew Bible prophet defended the worship of Yahweh against the cult of Baal, performed miracles including calling down fire from the sky, and is said to have ascended to heaven alive without dying — who was he?
Elijah: Biblical prophet. In 1 Kings 18, Elijah defended the worship of the Hebrew deity Yahweh over that of the Canaanite deity Baal.
In Greek myth, this Phoenician princess was abducted by a god disguised as a bull and became mother to Crete's King Minos — who was she?
Europa (consort of Zeus): Greek mythology character, daughter of Agenor.

First Republic of Armenia: 1918–1920 country in Western Asia.
This Japanese prime minister presided over the 1937 invasion of China and pushed through laws that turned his country into a totalitarian state before World War II — who is he?

Getúlio Vargas: President of Brazil (1930–1945; 1951–1954). Born on 19 April 1882 in São Borja, Rio Grande do Sul, to a powerful local family, Vargas had a short stint in the Brazilian Army before entering law school.
This Weimar-era German chancellor and foreign minister shared the 1926 Nobel Peace Prize with Aristide Briand for reconciling Germany and France — who was he?
Gustav Stresemann: Chancellor of Germany in 1923. After obtaining his doctorate, Stresemann worked in trade associations before entering politics.
Ruling Jordan since 1921 and tracing its lineage to the great-grandfather of the Islamic prophet Muhammad, which royal family once also held the thrones of Hejaz, Syria and Iraq?
Hashemites: Royal family of Jordan since 1921. The family belongs to the Dhawu Awn, one of the branches of the Ḥasanid Sharifs of Mecca, also referred to as Hashemites.
Spanning roughly 1000 to 1300 CE, this European era saw a population boom, the 12th-century renaissance, and the growth of cities before the Black Death struck — which period?
High Middle Ages: Period of European history between AD 1000 and 1350.

Human history: Records of Earth's people.
A conflict from 1922 to 1923 following Irish independence, fought between the Provisional Government of Ireland and the Anti-Treaty IRA over the Anglo-Irish Treaty. What is this?

Irish Civil War: 1922–1923 conflict between factions of the IRA. The National Army benefited from substantial quantities of weapons provided by the British government, particularly artillery and armoured cars.
Born in 2007 as the youngest grandchild of Queen Elizabeth II, this British royal was known by a viscount's title until 2023 and is a nephew of King Charles III — who is he?

At just 16, this Australian sailor spent seven months attempting a solo circumnavigation of the globe, an achievement later dramatized in the 2023 Netflix film True Spirit — who is she?

Popularly known by his initials, this politician served as Telangana's first Chief Minister for nearly a decade and founded the regional party Bharat Rashtra Samithi — who is he?
K. Chandrashekar Rao: 1st chief Minister of Telangana from 2014 to 2023.

Also known as Cheops, this Fourth Dynasty pharaoh is generally credited with commissioning one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World — yet survives in just one tiny complete ivory portrait. Who was he?
Khufu: Fourth Dynasty ancient Egyptian pharaoh. Khufu, or Cheops, was the second pharaoh of the Fourth Dynasty of Egypt, reigning during the 26th century BC in the early Old Kingdom period.

Founded in 2016 by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, this left-wing to far-left French party pushed an eco-socialist program called 'A Shared Future' and saw its founder narrowly miss the presidential runoff in 2017 — which party?
La France Insoumise: French political party. La France Insoumise (French: [la fʁɑ̃s ɛ̃sumiz], lit. 'France Unbowed'; LFI or FI) is a left-wing to far-left political party in France.
Founded in 1988 and currently led by Ed Davey, this UK political party is the third-largest in the House of Commons with 72 MPs — what is it?
Liberal Democrats (UK): British political party. The Liberal Democrats, colloquially known as the Lib Dems, is a political party in the United Kingdom.
A member of the Fang ethnic group who began as a colonial customs agent, he became the first Prime Minister and then President of Gabon, serving until his death in 1967 — who was he?
Léon M'ba: Prime Minister (1959–61) and President (1961–67) of Gabon.

Ruling Panama from 1983 to 1989 through puppet presidents while amassing a fortune in drug trafficking, this dictator was ousted by a U.S. invasion despite past ties to American intelligence — who was he?
Manuel Noriega: Military dictator of Panama from 1983 to 1989. Born in Panama City to a poor pardo family, Noriega studied at the Chorrillos Military School in Lima and at the School of the Americas.
Serving as president of an organization that advocates overthrowing Iran's government, which Iranian dissident politician was born in December 1953?
Founder of the agrarian movement AGROunia, this politician served as Poland's deputy minister of agriculture from 2023 to 2025 — who is he?
Michał Kołodziejczak: Polish politician. Michał Kołodziejczak (born 14 September 1988) is a Polish politician and founder of AGROunia.
This former Afghan president took shelter in a UN compound in Kabul after a failed flight to India, living there until the Taliban's 1996 capture of the city ended in his assassination — who was he?
Mohammad Najibullah: Leader of Afghanistan from 1987 to 1992.
Serving as Lebanon's prime minister across three separate terms since 2005, this politician lost his final bid for a fourth term in January 2025 to the ICJ president, 9 votes to 84 — who is he?
Najib Mikati: Prime Minister of Lebanon (born 1955)
Head of the Soviet secret police at the height of the Great Purge, this Stalin-era official orchestrated mass arrests and executions before being arrested and executed himself in 1940 — who was he?
Nikolai Yezhov: NKVD director under Joseph Stalin (1895–1940)
This was the U.S. military's codename for its multinational campaign against the Islamic State across Iraq, Syria, and Libya — which campaign?
Operation Inherent Resolve: Military intervention against the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant.
Born to minor Prussian nobility, he commanded the Imperial German Army in WWI and, though no friend of Nazism, as German president handed Hitler the chancellorship in 1933 — who was he?
Paul von Hindenburg: President of Germany from 1925 to 1934.
This Odawa war chief led Native Americans against the British in the Great Lakes region from 1763 to 1766, in a conflict that came to bear his name — who was he?
Pontiac (Odawa leader): 18th-century Native American war chief.

She served as France's Minister of Justice under Sarkozy before later becoming Minister of Culture across four different governments, and has been mayor of one of Paris's arrondissements since 2008. Who is this French politician?

Republic of Rose Island: 1968 micronation in the Adriatic Sea. The Italian government viewed it as a ploy by Rosa to raise money from tourists while avoiding national taxation.
This U.S. Army officer led E Company's assault on the Belgian town of Foy after the siege of Bastogne was broken, and later served as the American governor of a Berlin prison — who is he?

Born in Leptis Magna in Roman Africa, this general emerged as the final victor of the chaotic Year of the Five Emperors to rule Rome from 193 to 211 — who is he?
Septimius Severus: Roman emperor from 193 to 211. Lucius Septimius Severus (Latin: [ˈluːkius sepˈtimius seˈweːrus]; 11 April 145 – 4 February 211) was Roman emperor from 193 to 211.
Fought in two stages, a winter and summer campaign from 1614 to 1615, this conflict ended the Toyotomi clan and cemented Tokugawa rule over Japan — which historic clash?
Siege of Osaka: 1614-15 series of battles in Japan at the end of the Sengoku Period.

This doctrine holding that governing authority is legitimate to some degree — especially over taxation and production — gained traction in American political discourse during the 1930s and '40s, its opposite being anarchism — what's it called?

Statism: Doctrine that the political authority of the state is legitimate to some degree. In political science, statism or etatism (from French, état 'state') is the doctrine that the political authority of the state is legitimate to some degree.
Serving as Ottoman Grand Vizier during World War I, this convicted war criminal is remembered as the architect of the Armenian genocide — who was he?

Thomas Playford IV: 20th-century Australian politician and fruit grower (1896–1981)
The first Asian to lead the United Nations, this Burmese diplomat served a record ten years and one month as Secretary-General starting in 1961 — who was he?
U Thant: UN Secretary-General from 1961 to 1971.

Raiding, trading, and settling from Scandinavia across Europe, North Africa, and even Newfoundland between the late 8th and 11th centuries, this seafaring people helped establish Kievan Rus'. Who were they?
Vikings: Norse seafarers, merchants and raiders.
Launched by the United States after the September 11 attacks, this global campaign targeted al-Qaeda, the Taliban, and later Iraq's Ba'athist regime — what was it called?
War on terror: Military campaign following the September 11 attacks.
First achieved in Australasia before spreading to Europe and the Americas, this democratic right for female voters began its 'first wave' in 1893 in English-speaking countries — what right?
Women's suffrage: Legal right of women to vote.
Revered as the Father of the Nation, this ruler of Abu Dhabi became the first president of a newly unified Gulf federation in 1971?
Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan: President of the United Arab Emirates from 1971 to 2004.

COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is a physicist?
Louis Slotin is a physicist. Louis Alexander Slotin ( SLOHT-in; 1 December 1910 – 30 May 1946) was a Canadian physicist and chemist who took part in the Manhattan Project.
Pick the chemist from these four.
James Lovelock is a chemist. James Ephraim Lovelock (26 July 1919 – 26 July 2022) was an English independent scientist, environmentalist and futurist.
What is the atomic number of Unbiunium?
Unbiunium, also known as eka-actinium or element 121, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has symbol Ubu and atomic number 121.
In what year was J. Robert Oppenheimer born?
J. Robert Oppenheimer: In 1941, Oppenheimer was briefed about nuclear weapon design by Australian physicist Mark Oliphant.
In what year did Archimedes die?
Archimedes died during the siege of Syracuse, when he was killed by a Roman soldier despite orders that he should not be harmed.
In what year was Iron discovered?
Iron is a chemical element; it has symbol Fe (from Latin ferrum 'iron') and atomic number 26.
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. Designed by the Soviet Union's Mikoyan-Gurevich bureau, it is an aircraft built primarily using stainless steel.
Which country is Sukhoi Su-57 from?
Sukhoi Su-57: Russia. The Sukhoi Su-57 (Russian: Сухой Су-57; NATO reporting name: Felon) is a twin-engine stealth multirole fighter aircraft developed by Sukhoi.
Who is credited with discovering Gaussian integral?
Gaussian integral: Leonhard Euler. The integral has a wide range of applications.
Who is credited with discovering Aspirin?
Aspirin: Raffaele Piria. Aspirin is used to treat inflammatory conditions including Kawasaki disease, pericarditis, and rheumatic fever.
Who is credited with discovering Boron?
Boron: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac. Boron is a chemical element; it has symbol B and atomic number 5.

The active component of vinegar and the second simplest carboxylic acid, this colourless liquid with the formula CH₃COOH has been produced in large quantities since the third millennium BCE. What is this acid?
Acetic acid is an acidic, colourless liquid and organic compound with the chemical formula CH3COOH (also written as CH3CO2H, C2H4O2, or HC2H3O2).
A military pilot who became the first astronaut representing Turkey, he reached the International Space Station on 18 January 2024 aboard the Axiom Mission 3 flight — who is he?
Alper Gezeravcı (born 2 December 1979) is a military pilot and the first Turkish astronaut.
What term describes the discipline of measuring human body dimensions, applied everywhere from ergonomics and architecture to tracking historical living standards?
Anthropometry (from Ancient Greek (nthrpos) 'human' and (mtron) 'measure') refers to the measurement of the human individual.

Distinguished from celestial mechanics by asking what heavenly bodies ARE rather than where they are, this science applies physics and chemistry to the Sun, stars, galaxies, and exoplanets — which discipline?
Astrophysics is a science that applies the methods and principles of physics and chemistry in the study of astronomical objects and phenomena including the universe.
This steroid medication treats conditions ranging from rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis to asthma, and is also given before preterm birth to help speed a baby's lung development — what drug is it?
Betamethasone is a steroid medication. It can be taken by mouth, injected into a muscle, or applied to the skin, typically in cream, lotion, or liquid forms.

Derived from Greek words for 'slow' and 'heart', this medical term describes a resting heart rate under 60 beats per minute — sometimes a red flag, sometimes just a sign of a well-conditioned athlete. Name the condition?
Bradycardia (brads), meaning "slow", and (karda), meaning "heart", also called bradyarrhythmia, is a resting heart rate under 60 beats per minute (BPM).
Caused by an overgrowth of a common yeast, this fungal infection is known as thrush when it affects the mouth and can also cause a genital yeast infection — name the condition?
Candidiasis is a fungal infection due to any species of yeasts in the genus Candida or those that were formerly classified in genus Candida but are now classified in the genus Candidozyma.
Despite no clinical evidence it treats any disease, this daisy-like plant is a staple in calming herbal tea, beer brewing, and even garden ground cover — what is it?
Chamomile (American English) or camomile (British English; see spelling differences) (or) is the common name for several daisy-like plants of the family Asteraceae.
Born near Toulouse, this French inventor is remembered chiefly as an aviation pioneer — though in 1870 he was also an early enthusiast of cycling in France; who was he?
Clément Ader (French; 2 April 1841 - 3 May 1925) was a French inventor and engineer who was born near Toulouse in Muret, Haute-Garonne, and died in Toulouse.
Going by puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther depending on the region, this big cat is the most widely distributed wild land mammal in the Western Hemisphere — what is it?
Cougar (Puma concolor), also called puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther, is a large feline native to the Americas.
Caused by either too little insulin or cells that ignore it, this condition keeps blood sugar stubbornly high and comes chiefly in a type 1 and a type 2 — what is it?
Diabetes is a group of common endocrine diseases characterized by sustained high blood sugar levels.
This social science examines the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services, analyzing everything from individual agents to entire economies. What discipline is this?
Economics is a social science that studies the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services.
This class of mental health condition is defined by an enduring, pervasive pattern of behavior, emotion, and thought that deviates from social norms and develops early in life. What is it?
Erythritol is an organic compound, the naturally occurring achiral meso four-carbon sugar alcohol (or polyol).
Which evergreen conifer genus has needle-like leaves attached singly to the branch by a circular base, and cones that stand upright like a cedar's rather than hanging down? What is it?
Fir are evergreen coniferous trees belonging to the genus Abies in the family Pinaceae.
Native to Pacific coastal waters from Alaska to Baja California, this giant burrowing clam can grow a siphon over three feet long and live for more than a century — which creature?
Geoduck (Panopea generosa) is a species of very large saltwater clam in the family Hiatellidae.

These common coastal seabirds, most closely related to terns and skimmers, were once known by an older name still surviving in some English dialects and cognate with the German word Möwe — what birds are they?
Gull (see Taxonomy), are seabirds of the subfamily Larinae.
First identified in 1910, this organic compound is stored in mast cells and basophils and, though not made by classic endocrine glands, still acts as a local hormone — what compound is it?
Histamine is an organic nitrogenous compound found in mammals and many vegetables, fruits and food products.

For decades this University of Virginia psychiatrist ran a Division of Perceptual Studies and gathered evidence that memories — and even bodily features — might carry across lives. Which researcher into reincarnation was he?

Ian Stevenson (October 31, 1918 - February 8, 2007) was a Canadian-born American psychiatrist, the founder and director of the Division of Perceptual Studies at the University of Virginia School of Medicine.

This American scientist co-authored a landmark 1953 paper with Francis Crick proposing the double-helix structure of DNA, building on research by Rosalind Franklin, and shared a 1962 Nobel Prize for the discovery — who is he?
James Watson (April 6, 1928 - November 6, 2025) was an American molecular biologist, geneticist, and zoologist.

Sharing the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, this ethologist was among the first to decode the honey bee's waggle dance — a theory greeted with such skepticism that it took decades to be vindicated. Who was he?
Karl von Frisch (20 November 1886 - 12 June 1982) was a German-Austrian ethologist who received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973, along with Nikolaas Tinbergen and Konrad Lorenz.

This Hungarian-born physicist conceived the nuclear chain reaction in 1933, drafted the famous letter Einstein signed to launch the Manhattan Project, then later petitioned President Truman not to drop the bomb on civilians — who was he?

Leo Szilard (born Le Spitz; February 11, 1898 - May 30, 1964) was a Hungarian-born American physicist, biologist and inventor who made numerous important discoveries in nuclear physics and the biological sciences.
Reclassified in 2021 as part of the order Psocodea alongside booklice and barklice, these tiny wingless parasites cement their eggs to a single host for life — what are they called?
Louse (pl.: lice) is the common name for any member of the infraorder Phthiraptera, which contains nearly 5,000 species of wingless parasitic insects.
Google's employee No. 20 and its first woman software engineer, she later left to run a famous internet company as CEO from 2012 until Verizon bought it — who is she?
Marissa Mayer (born May 30, 1975) is an American business executive, software engineer, and investor who served as president and chief executive officer of Yahoo!
What neurological disorder causes moderate-to-severe, often one-sided headaches, frequently accompanied by nausea, light and sound sensitivity, and sometimes preceded by a sensory 'aura'?
Migraine is a neurological disorder that causes moderate-to-severe headaches. The pain usually affects one side of the head.
With somewhere between 66 and 70 species across nine subfamilies, this carnivore family stretches from tiny weasels all the way up to the wolverine. What is it?
Mustelidae (from Latin mustela, weasel) are a diverse family of carnivoran mammals, including weasels, badgers, otters, sea otters, polecats, martens, grisons and wolverines.

Considered primary if a child has never had a long dry stretch, this common childhood condition — usually a developmental delay rather than an illness — is commonly called bedwetting. What's its clinical name?
Nocturnal enuresis (NE), also informally called bedwetting, is involuntary urination while asleep after the age at which bladder control usually begins.
Derived from an ancient Roman unit called the uncia, this unit of mass equals 1/16 of a pound in its common form, though a heavier 'troy' version weighs precious metals — name the unit?
Ounce is any of several different units of mass, weight, or volume and is derived almost unchanged from the uncia, an Ancient Roman unit of measurement.

This short-acting barbiturate is used as a sedative and anticonvulsant in low doses, but in high doses causes fatal respiratory arrest, making it a drug of choice for both veterinary euthanasia and U.S. executions — what is it?
Pentobarbital (US) or pentobarbitone (British and Australian) is a short-acting barbiturate typically used as a sedative, a preanesthetic, and to control convulsions in emergencies.
Native to Eurasia and identifiable by short, blue-green needles, this member of the pine family goes by several regional common names — name the species (Latin binomial)?
Pinus sylvestris is a species of tree in the pine family Pinaceae that is native to Eurasia.
Split into the strepsirrhines — lemurs and lorisids — and the haplorhines — tarsiers, monkeys and apes — this order ranges in size down to tiny Madame Berthe's — what is it?

Primate is an order of mammals, which is further divided into the strepsirrhines, which include lemurs, galagos, and lorisids; and the haplorhines, which include tarsiers and simians (monkeys and apes).

Founding an organization promoting swadeshi economics against globalization, this Indian social activist later allied with a yoga guru to combine that economic message with the promotion of yoga and Ayurveda — who is he?
Rajiv Dixit (30 November 1967 - 30 November 2010) was an Indian social activist who founded the Azadi Bachao Andolan.

This English X-ray crystallographer's photographs were crucial to unraveling the structure of DNA, yet her contribution went largely unrecognized in her lifetime, earning her posthumous nicknames like "the wronged heroine" — who was she?
Rosalind Franklin (25 July 1920 - 16 April 1958) was an English chemist and X-ray crystallographer.
With segmented bony armor, an upright posture, and a curling prehensile tail, these 46 species of tiny bony fish are cousins to the pipefishes and seadragons — what are they?
Seahorse (also written sea-horse and sea horse) is any of 46 species of small marine bony fish in the genus Hippocampus.
Once placed alone in the genus Uncia before phylogenetics moved it into Panthera, this high-altitude cat ranges across the Tibetan Plateau and Himalayas — what is it?
Snow leopard (Panthera uncia) is a species of large cat in the genus Panthera of the family Felidae.
Lacking the powder down that herons and ibises use to clean off fish slime, these bill-clattering wading birds come in 20 living species across six genera — which birds?
Stork are large, long-legged, long-necked wading birds with long, stout bills.

Equal to one weber per square metre, this SI unit of magnetic flux density was adopted in 1960 and named for a Serbian-American electrical engineer, on the proposal of a Slovenian engineer — name this unit?
Tesla (unit) (symbol: T) is the unit of magnetic flux density (B) (also called magnetic B-field) in the International System of Units (SI).
Roughly eight times more potent than an older analogue, this bleeding-control medication is also prescribed for hereditary angioedema — what is it?
Tranexamic acid is a medication used to treat or prevent excessive blood loss from major trauma, postpartum bleeding, surgery, tooth removal, nosebleeds, and heavy menstruation.
This British-American structural biologist shared the 2009 Nobel in Chemistry for revealing the ribosome's structure and later led the Royal Society as president — who is he?
Venki Ramakrishnan (born 1952) is a British-American structural biologist.
Marketed under names like Rompun, this veterinary sedative and alpha-2 adrenergic agonist is often combined with ketamine for animal anesthesia and used as an emetic in cats — what is it?

Xylazine is a structural analog of clonidine and an 2-adrenergic receptor agonist, sold under many trade names worldwide, most notably the Bayer brand name Rompun, as well as Anased, Sedazine and Chanazine.
Caused by a mutation in the FGFR3 gene, this genetic disorder is the most common cause of short stature, marked by shortened limbs, a normal-length torso and a prominent forehead — what is it called?
Achondroplasia: Genetic condition, the most common form of dwarfism.
With wingspans reaching up to eleven and a half feet, which large seabird family ranges across the Southern Ocean and North Pacific but is absent from the North Atlantic?
Albatross: Family of large seabirds. The albatrosses are usually regarded as falling into four genera, but disagreement exists over the number of species.
The heaviest member of its family, this Southeastern U.S. reptile sees males stretch up to 15 feet and tip 1,000 pounds — and it's the larger of just two surviving species in its genus. What is it?
American alligator: Crocodilian native to the Southeastern United States.

Characterized by extreme food restriction and a fear of gaining weight despite being underweight, this eating disorder is described in the DSM-5 as involving a disturbance in how one perceives their own body shape — what's the condition called?
Anorexia nervosa: Eating disorder. Individuals with anorexia nervosa have a fear of gaining weight, despite the fact that they are typically underweight.
Sold under the brand name Abilify, this atypical antipsychotic treats schizophrenia, bipolar mania, and irritability linked to autism spectrum disorder — what is it?
Aripiprazole: Atypical antipsychotic medication. Aripiprazole is taken by mouth or via injection into a muscle.
Delivered to the RAF starting in 1956, this delta-wing strategic bomber was considered the most advanced but riskiest of Britain's three V bombers — which aircraft?
Avro Vulcan: British jet-powered delta wing strategic bomber.
A largely self-taught naturalist and astronomer born to a free mother in Maryland, he helped survey the District of Columbia and corresponded with Thomas Jefferson — who was he?
Benjamin Banneker: American scientist, surveyor and farmer (1731–1806)
Despite being just 12 to 20 cm long, this small marine creature's vivid markings flash brighter when it feels threatened, and its bite delivers a neurotoxin called tetrodotoxin — what is it?
Blue-ringed octopus: Four species of mollusk.

Unique among mammals, human females are the only ones to permanently develop this secondary sex organ at puberty rather than just during pregnancy, and it later produces milk via the mammary gland — which body part?
Breast: Part of the female primate torso that has mammary glands.
With the formula CaC2, this industrial compound reacts with trace moisture to give off a garlicky smell and is used to generate acetylene gas in old-fashioned lamps — what is it?
Calcium carbide: Chemical compound. Its main use industrially is in the production of acetylene and calcium cyanamide.
This mammalian order of flesh-eating species is split into cat-like and dog-like suborders, Feliformia and Caniformia, and ranks as the sixth-largest order of mammals — which order?
Carnivora: Order of mammals. Carnivora ( kar-NIV-ər-ə) is an order of placental mammals specialised primarily in eating flesh, whose members are formally referred to as carnivorans.
Known in North America as fireweed and in Britain as rosebay willowherb, this perennial flowering plant thrives across the boreal forests of the Northern Hemisphere — which plant?
Chamaenerion angustifolium: Species of flowering plant in the willowherb family.

Native to Sri Lanka, the inner bark of this evergreen tree is the original source of a beloved baking spice, sometimes distinguished from a cheaper cousin as the 'true' or 'Ceylon' variety — which tree?
Cinnamomum verum: Species of tree. The inner bark of the tree is historically regarded as the spice cinnamon, though this term was later generalized to include C. cassia as well.
Also known as foremilk or historically as 'beestings,' this early substance produced by mammary glands right after birth delivers antibodies and immune factors to newborns. What is it?
Colostrum: Form of milk produced immediately following the delivery of newborn.
First described in 1880 by a French neurologist, this rare delusion convinces sufferers that they are dead, don't exist, or have lost their internal organs — what is it called?
Cotard's syndrome: Delusion that one is dead or non-existent.
Bred in Germany with short legs and a long body to chase badgers into their burrows, which hound breed comes in smooth-, wire-, and long-haired varieties?

Historically defined by having two embryonic seed leaves, this once-standard division of flowering plants covers around 200,000 species but turned out not to share one common ancestor — which plant group?
Dicotyledon: Historical grouping of flowering plants.
This first section of the small intestine, often the principal site of iron absorption, connects the stomach to the middle portion of the intestine — what is it?
Duodenum: First section of the small intestine. The duodenum is the first section of the small intestine in most vertebrates, including mammals, reptiles, and birds.
A Swedish scientist and inventor until, at 53, dreams and visions sent him into a spiritual phase, this polymath became best known for his 1758 book on the afterlife, Heaven and Hell — who was he?
Emanuel Swedenborg: Swedish scientist, philosopher, and theologian (1688–1772)
With a sweet smell like pear drops, this colorless solvent turns up in nail-polish remover and is used to decaffeinate tea and coffee. What is it?
Named after a 19th-century English physicist, this SI unit measures a material's ability to store electrical charge, equal to one coulomb per volt — what is it?
Farad: SI unit of electric capacitance.
Patented in 1962 and sold under a brand name synonymous with 'roofies,' this benzodiazepine is notoriously linked to date-rape drug use — what is it?
Flunitrazepam: Benzodiazepine sedative. Flunitrazepam, sold under the brand name Rohypnol among others, is a benzodiazepine used to treat severe insomnia and assist with anesthesia.
Born in Pisa in 1564, this Italian polymath has been crowned the father of observational astronomy and the scientific method — and was among the earliest tinkerers to build a thermoscope. Who is he?
Galileo Galilei: Italian physicist and astronomer (1564–1642)

This Italian friar and cosmological theorist proposed that stars were distant suns with their own planets, and was tried for heresy by the Roman Inquisition for insisting the universe is infinite — who was he?
Giordano Bruno: Italian Dominican friar, philosopher and mathematician (1548–1600)
This junctional area between the torso and thigh, where the lower abdominal wall meets the leg, is commonly strained in a familiar sports injury — what is it called?
Groin: Area between the torso and the thigh. In human anatomy, the groin, also known as the inguinal region or iliac region, is the junctional area between the torso and the thigh.
This wingless insect spends its entire life on the human scalp, sipping blood, and can neither fly nor jump — its short stumpy legs can't even walk well on a flat surface. What tiny freeloader is it?
Head louse: Insect parasite of humans.
Also called urticaria, this skin condition brings red or flesh-colored raised, itchy bumps that may sting and often follow an allergic reaction — what is it?
Hives: Skin disease characterized by red, raised, and itchy bumps.
Named from Greek words meaning "over" and "formation," this condition enlarges tissue by increasing the number of cells rather than their size — which term, distinct from hypertrophy?
Hyperplasia: Enlargement of tissue due to cell proliferation.
This sugar alcohol, with about half the sweetness of table sugar, is made by the human kidney at roughly two grams a day and reaches its highest concentration in the brain — what is it?
Inositol: Carbocyclic sugar. Its formula is C6H12O6; the molecule has a ring of six carbon atoms, each with a hydrogen atom and a hydroxy group (–OH).
This fragrant genus of shrubs and vines in the olive family is grown in vast quantities in one Egyptian village that supplies much of the world's perfume industry — which plant?
Jasmine: Genus of flowering plant in the olive family Oleaceae.
Born Giulia Maddalena Angela in Italy, this physician became a leading freethinker and activist for women's rights and social reform in early-20th-century Argentina — who is she?
Julieta Lanteri: Argentine doctor and activist (1873–1932)
Biosynthesized in the body from the amino acid tyrosine, this compound is the direct precursor to dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine — what is it?
L-DOPA: Chemical compound. As is true for many molecules, the human body produces only one of these isomers (the l-DOPA form).

Elon Musk's praise for his MIT driver-attention study on Tesla's autopilot brought this computer scientist to prominence in 2019, ahead of a career hosting long-form interviews with notable figures — who is he?
Lex Fridman: American scientist and podcast host (born 1983)
Sold under the brand name Cozaar, this angiotensin receptor blocker treats high blood pressure while also protecting the kidneys in diabetic patients — what drug is it?
Losartan: Blood pressure medication. Losartan, sold under the brand name Cozaar among others, is a medication used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension).
Known by the common English name 'mallow,' this plant genus bears palmately lobed leaves and five-petaled flowers ranging from pink to white — which genus?

Marked by small white Koplik spots inside the mouth and a red rash that starts on the face before spreading, this highly contagious, vaccine-preventable disease can bring fevers over 40°C — which disease?
This theoretical physicist and science communicator bridged science and science fiction well enough to win a 2021 lifetime achievement award named for Arthur C. Clarke — who is he?
Michio Kaku: American theoretical physicist, futurist and author.

Thought to enjoy 'hybrid vigor' and a reduced risk of inbreeding-linked health problems, this catch-all term covers roughly 150 million dogs worldwide that don't belong to any officially recognized breed — what's it called?
Named for its resemblance to a tiny mouse's ear, this flowering plant genus is known in the Northern Hemisphere by a romantic common name and is Alaska's official flower — what is it?
Myosotis: Genus of flowering plants in the family Boraginaceae.
This synthetic element 113 was claimed by both a Russian-American team at Dubna and, in 2004, a Japanese team at Riken. What's its name?
Nihonium: Chemical element with atomic number 113 (Nh)

Distinct from an unrelated American family with a similar name, these small seed-eating birds include house- and tree-dwelling species that nest on buildings in huge city numbers — which bird family is this?
Old World sparrow: Family of songbirds. Old World sparrows are groups of small passerine birds forming the family Passeridae.
Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1993, this scripting language's name began as 'Personal Home Page' before becoming a recursive backronym meaning 'Hypertext Preprocessor' — what is it?
PHP: Scripting language created in 1994. PHP is a general-purpose scripting language geared towards web development.
Derived from Greek words meaning 'healer of children,' this branch of medicine covers care from infancy through adolescence — what is it?
Pediatrics: Branch of medicine caring for children. Within the Commonwealth, pediatrics covers patients until the age of 18, except in India where the pediatric age is 12.
Formed by stripping three protons from phosphoric acid, this triply-charged ion carries the formula PO4³⁻ and lends its name to esters like trimethyl ester in organic chemistry — what anion is it?
Phosphate: Anion, salt, functional group or ester derived from a phosphoric acid.
Named after a French mathematician and physicist, this materials-science measure captures how much a material bulges sideways when compressed lengthwise — what is it?
Poisson's ratio: Measure of material deformation perpendicular to loading.

Diagnosed in about 8% of male urology visits in the US, this umbrella term covers several bacterial and non-bacterial pelvic conditions, despite its name not always involving actual inflammation — which condition?
Prostatitis: Medical condition. Prostatitis is an umbrella term for a variety of medical conditions that incorporate bacterial and non-bacterial origin illnesses in the pelvic region.
Named partly for Jack Northrop, designer of a tailless aircraft, which genus of enormous azhdarchid pterosaur is a top candidate for the largest flying animal ever?
Quetzalcoatlus: Genus of azhdarchid pterosaurs from the Late Cretaceous.

Marked by tea-colored urine and triggered by crush injuries or extreme exertion, this condition involves skeletal muscle breaking down so fast that released myoglobin can damage the kidneys — what is it called?
Rhabdomyolysis: Condition in which damaged skeletal muscle breaks down rapidly.
What term describes herbivorous mammals like cattle and giraffes that digest plant matter by regurgitating and re-chewing it as cud?
Ruminant: Hoofed herbivorous grazing or browsing mammals.
Driven by an empirical cycle of observation, hypothesis, testing, and conclusion, this systematic discipline splits into natural and social branches. What is it?
Science: Systematic endeavour to gain knowledge.
Also called herpes zoster, this viral disease paints a painful blistering rash down just one side of the body, and can leave lingering nerve pain called postherpetic neuralgia — what is it?
Shingles: Viral disease caused by the varicella zoster virus.

Known as sun spiders, camel spiders, or wind scorpions, this arachnid order is neither true spider nor scorpion, and urban legends wildly exaggerate its size, speed, and danger to humans — what is it?
Solifugae: Order of arachnids. The order includes more than 1,000 described species in about 147 genera.
Fired by Apple's board in 1985, he founded NeXT and bought a animation studio before returning a decade later to revolutionize consumer tech. Who?
Steve Jobs: American businessman and inventor (1955–2011)
Serving as prime minister of Turkey seven separate times before becoming president from 1993 to 2000, he was also the first PM to have been born in the Turkish Republic — who was he?

Süleyman Demirel: President of Turkey from 1993 to 2000. Demirel was the leader of the opposition from 1971 to 1975 before forming a right-wing government known as the First Nationalist Front, which collapsed in 1977.
With more than 8,000 species known for their loud mating calls and leaf-like camouflage, this insect family also goes by the common name katydids or bush crickets — which family?
Tettigoniidae: Family of insects. Insects in the family Tettigoniidae are commonly called katydids (especially in North America) or bush crickets.
This colorless solvent's sweet smell partly explains the aroma of gasoline and paint fumes, and its IUPAC name is simply methylbenzene — which aromatic hydrocarbon is it?
Toluene: Aromatic hydrocarbon. Toluene is a colorless, water-insoluble liquid with a sweet smell, and is partially responsible for the aroma of gasoline and paint fumes.
First flown in 1952, this nuclear-capable Soviet bomber is the only turboprop strategic bomber still flying — its contra-rotating propellers earning it the NATO nickname 'Bear.' What is it?
Tupolev Tu-95: Russian strategic bomber aircraft.
This hairy biennial plant can top two meters, packing small yellow flowers onto a tall spike that sprouts from a low leaf rosette in disturbed, sunlit soil — which weedy species?
Verbascum thapsus: Species of plant. It is a hairy biennial plant that can grow to 2 m tall or more.

Distinguished by its wide, square-lipped mouth built for grazing, this is the largest and most social species in its family; its northern subspecies lost its last known male, Sudan, in 2018 — which animal?
White rhinoceros: Species of large land mammal.
Tracing its formal origins to Aristotle and later shaped by Carl Linnaeus, this branch of biology studies the structure, classification and behavior of animals — which field?
The symbol for hassium is Hs. Hassium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Hs and atomic number 108.
The symbol for actinium is Ac. Actinium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ac and atomic number 89.

John Leguizamo (born 1960) is the earliest of the four. John Alberto Leguizamo Peláez (LEG-wih-ZAH-moh; Colombian Spanish: [leɣiˈsamo]; born July 22, 1960) is an American stand-up comedian, actor, and film producer.
Which of these four is the eldest?

Indiana Jones (character) (born 1899) is the earliest of the four. Henry Walton "Indiana" Jones, Jr., often called "Indy" for short, is the title character and protagonist of the Indiana Jones franchise.
Robin Hood (founded 1370) is the earliest of the four.

Robin Hood (founded 1370) is the earliest of the four. Robin Hood is a legendary heroic outlaw originally depicted in English folklore and subsequently featured in literature, theatre, and cinema.

The Turbo Charged Prelude for 2 Fast 2 Furious

In what year was Macaulay Culkin born?
Macaulay Culkin: Macaulay Macaulay Culkin Culkin (born Macaulay Carson Culkin; August 26, 1980 (1980-08-26)) is an American actor and musician.
In what year was Bill Hader born?
Bill Hader: William Thomas Hader Jr. (born June 7, 1978) is an American actor, comedian, and filmmaker.
In what year was Jamie Foxx born?
Jamie Foxx: Eric Marlon Bishop (born December 13, 1967), known professionally as Jamie Foxx, is an American actor, comedian, singer, and film producer.
